                                        PROJECT NO. 58481
      RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
     LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
     STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §                    OF TEXAS
                                                     §

HIF USA LLC’S COMMENTS ON THE COMMISSION’S PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION
        TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS



HIF USA LLC (“HIF”) respectfully submits the following comments in response to the Public

Utility Commission of Texas's rulemaking proceeding to implement large load interconnection

standards under PURA § 37.0561. These comments address three discrete issues related to Batch

Zero eligibility, the applicability of financial security and fee requirements to demonstrably

ready projects, and the refundability of financial security posted in connection with intermediate

agreements.

1.       Projects with demonstrated readiness should qualify for Batch Zero as Base Load

      The Commission should designate projects in Batch Zero as Base Load that have already

advanced substantially through the interconnection process. Specifically, a project should qualify

for Batch Zero as Base Load if it has, at minimum: (1) an executed interconnection agreement

with the applicable Transmission and Distribution Service Provider (“TDSP”); (2) posted

financial security as required under that agreement; (3) funded Contribution in Aid of

Construction (“CIAC”) payments in accordance with TDSP-determined interconnection costs;

(4) ordered major electrical equipment necessary for the project; and (5) completed applicable

interconnection studies.

      These criteria reflect a meaningful, objective threshold of project maturity. A project

satisfying all five conditions has moved well beyond conceptual planning; it has made binding
 financial commitments, procured long-lead equipment, and cleared the interconnection study

queue. Excluding such projects from Batch Zero as Base Load would ignore the substantial and

verifiable steps they have already taken in reliance on existing regulatory frameworks.

   Additionally, the Commission should treat inclusion in ERCOT's Reliability Transmission

Planning (“RTP”) in the prior year(s) as a relevant and favorable indicator when evaluating

Batch Zero Base Load eligibility. Inclusion of the project in the RTP reflects that ERCOT has

independently identified the project's load as a factor in transmission planning, a strong

corroborating signal of project credibility and proximity to energization. While RTP inclusion

should not be required, it provides useful, readily verifiable evidence that the Commission

should be permitted to consider in making Batch Zero Base Load determinations.



   2. The $50,000/MW financial security and interconnection fee requirements should not

apply to projects that have already demonstrated readiness and should not be applied

retroactively to executed TDSP interconnection agreements

   The proposed rulemaking contemplates two distinct financial obligations: $50,000/MW in

financial security at the intermediate agreement stage and a non-refundable $50,000/MW fee at

the interconnection agreement stage. Neither should apply to projects that have already executed

a TDSP interconnection agreement, established site control, posted financial security, and funded

CIAC payments. Such projects have already demonstrated the commitment these requirements

are designed to elicit. Imposing additional obligations on them would produce no incremental

reliability benefit, create unforeseen capital burdens on projects well advanced in the

development cycle, and run contrary to cost causation principles and the objectives of SB 6.
      Neither obligation should be applied retroactively to projects with interconnection

agreements already executed with a TDSP prior to the effective date of this rulemaking. Projects

that structured their development timelines and capital plans under the prior regulatory

framework, particularly those with an assigned LLIS number and a history of significant TDSP

payments, including study costs and CIAC, have earned a degree of regulatory certainty that

retroactive fees and security requirements would undermine.

     Furthermore, the proposed $50,000/MW obligation, whether structured as a non-refundable

fee or financial security, is prohibitively high and risks excluding entrepreneurs and smaller

developers from pursuing large load projects in Texas. A lower threshold would still achieve the

Commission's goal of ensuring meaningful financial commitment while preserving a competitive

and accessible development market.

     The Commission should expressly provide that: (1) the $50,000/MW interconnection

agreement fee and intermediate agreement financial security is an obligation that should not

apply to projects with executed TDSP interconnection agreements, site control, posted security,

and funded CIAC; (2) neither obligation applies retroactively to agreements already executed as

of the effective date of the new rules; and (3) consider a lower threshold for the obligation that

achieves financial commitment without constraining the competitive development market within

Texas.

3.       Financial security posted at the intermediate agreement stage should be fully

refundable

         To the extent the Commission retains a financial security requirement applicable to the

intermediate agreement stage, any such security should be fully refundable. The intermediate
 agreement is executed prior to the conclusion of transmission system planning studies. This

requirement forces developers to commit significant capital based on assumptions about system

capability that cannot be confirmed until after the Batch Study process is completed. A large load

project at the intermediate agreement stage does not have a clear line of sight to timing of

energization, and therefore no ability to accurately assess whether or to what degree it will

proceed to interconnection.

       Requiring non-refundable financial security at a point in the process when project

viability cannot yet be meaningfully evaluated would impose a harsh and disproportionate

penalty on projects that ultimately do not proceed for reasons entirely outside their control,

including adverse study outcomes, transmission constraints identified in subsequent studies, or

grid-related factors that are not knowable until after the studies are complete. A fully refundable

security structure appropriately allocates this risk: it maintains an incentive for good-faith

engagement while ensuring that projects are not penalized for circumstances that could not have

been anticipated at the time the intermediate agreement was executed.

       The Commission should therefore provide expressly that financial security posted in

connection with an intermediate agreement is fully refundable if the project does not proceed to

execution of an interconnection agreement, regardless of the reason for non-proceeding.




       HIF appreciates the Commission's attention to these issues and respectfully urges

adoption of the positions set forth above. A well-designed Batch Zero framework and

appropriately calibrated financial security and fee structure will ensure that projects that have

already demonstrated meaningful commitment are not disadvantaged relative to projects at
 earlier stages of development, while continuing to advance the Commission's goals of an orderly

and reliable interconnection queue.




Date: April 16, 2026

Respectfully submitted,
Mason Galanski
Director, Power
HIF USA LLC
                                  PUC PROJECT NO. 58481
                          HIF USA LLC’S INITIAL COMMENTS
                                  EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


•   Batch Zero Base Load Eligibility
       o Projects that have executed a TDSP interconnection agreement, posted financial
          security, funded CIAC payments, ordered major equipment, and completed applicable
          studies should qualify for Batch Zero as Base Load
       o These criteria reflect binding financial commitments and meaningful project maturity,
          not speculative intent
•   $50,000/MW fee and security requirements
       o The $50,000/MW intermediate agreement security and non-refundable $50,000/MW
          interconnection agreement fee is an obligation that should not apply to projects with
          an existing executed TDSP interconnection agreement, site control, posted security,
          and funded CIAC
       o Neither obligation should be imposed retroactively on agreements already executed
          prior to the effective date of the new rules
       o Consider a lower threshold for the required obligation (<$50,000/MW) to ensure
          financial commitment while also maintaining a competitive development market
•   Intermediate agreement security must be fully refundable
       o The intermediate agreement precedes the conclusion of transmission planning studies
          required in the batch study process, so projects have low visibility into study
          outcomes or interconnection feasibility at this stage
       o Non-refundable security at this point penalizes projects for unknowable
          circumstances and should be fully refundable
